summary: This Standards Track document specifies the architecture, signaling, and procedures for Point-to-Multipoint Policies in Segment Routing, for both SR-MPLS and SRv6. It defines the policy construct, its candidate paths, and the instantiation of P2MP tree instances for efficient multipoint delivery. It updates RFC 9524.

plainLanguage.summary: Copying a packet once at the entrance and sending the copies all the way to every destination wastes bandwidth, because the copies share the same path for much of the journey. This document builds the tree instead, so copies are made along the way at the points where the tree branches. A policy names the entrance and the destinations, and a controller works out the shape of the tree and installs it on the routers.

questions: what is an sr p2mp policy
what is a p2mp tree instance
subtitle: How a Segment Routing domain builds a tree for multipoint traffic, and copies packets only where the tree branches.

tldr.problem: A multipoint service built from a single replication segment copies every packet at the ingress and sends the copies the whole way, even though the copies share most of their path, which wastes bandwidth on the shared links.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the SR P2MP Policy, a construct that names a Root node and a set of Leaf nodes, holds one or more candidate paths, and produces P2MP tree instances. A tree instance is a set of Replication segments stitched together, with a Replication segment at the Root, at intermediate Replication nodes and at the Leaf nodes.
tldr.outcome: The document defines the identifiers used for policies, candidate paths and tree instances, how traffic is steered into a policy with a Binding SID or local forwarding policy, and what a controller must do to compute and install a tree. It updates the Replication-ID of RFC 9524 and needs no IANA registrations.

facts.label: Policy identifier
facts.value: The Root address and the Tree-ID

today: RFC 9960 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2026. It updates RFC 9524, which defines the Replication segment that this document builds into trees. The signalling itself is not part of this document: it points to work in progress on PCEP, BGP and YANG extensions for the SR P2MP Policy, and it needs no IANA registrations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 9524 defines a Replication segment, which lets a node in a Segment Routing (SR) domain copy traffic to several downstream nodes. A Point-to-Multipoint (P2MP) service can be built from a single Replication segment running from the ingress node to all the egress nodes of the service. The document calls this ingress replication, and it is inefficient, because the traffic of the service may travel over the same set of nodes and links on its way from the ingress node to the egress nodes.

A multipoint service is delivered more efficiently as a tree. A P2MP tree runs from a Root node to a set of Leaf nodes through intermediate Replication nodes. It consists of a Replication segment at the Root node, and that segment is stitched to one or more Replication segments between the Leaf nodes and the intermediate Replication nodes. A Bud node is a node that is both a Replication node and a Leaf node, and the document uses the term Leaf node to include Bud nodes.

An SR P2MP Policy defines the Root and the Leaf nodes of the tree. It has one or more candidate paths, each with optional constraints or optimisation objectives. A controller computes a P2MP tree instance for a candidate path and then installs it in the SR domain by signalling Replication segments to the Root, Replication and Leaf nodes. The Replication segments of an instance can be built for either the SR-MPLS or the SRv6 data plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Copying a packet once at the entrance and sending the copies all the way to every destination wastes bandwidth, because the copies share the same path for much of the journey. This document builds the tree instead: copies are made along the way, at the points where the tree branches. A policy names the entrance and the destinations, and a controller works out the shape of the tree and installs it.

sections.title: The Terms: Policy, Candidate Path and Tree Instance
sections.content:
The document defines its own terms in Section 1.1.

  • An SR P2MP Policy is a framework for constructing P2MP trees in an SR domain by specifying the Root and Leaf nodes.
  • The Tree-ID identifies an SR P2MP Policy in the context of the Root node.
  • A candidate path of the policy defines the topological or resource constraints and the optimisation objectives used to compute and construct tree instances.
  • A P2MP tree instance (PTI) is constructed by stitching Replication segments between the Root and the Leaf nodes of the policy. Its topology is determined by the constraints and optimisation objective of the candidate path. The Instance-ID identifies a tree instance in the context of the policy.
  • The Tree-SID is the Replication-SID of the Replication segment at the Root node of a tree instance.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy is the plan. The candidate path says what the plan requires, for example which paths to avoid. The tree instance is the result: the actual set of routes that carries the traffic. The identifiers are the policy's number, the instance's number and the number of the route that enters the tree.

sections.title: Identifiers and Components of a Policy
sections.content:
An SR P2MP Policy is uniquely identified by the tuple <Root, Tree-ID>, where Root is the IP address of the Root node and Tree-ID is a 32-bit unsigned integer that is unique in the context of that Root. A policy holds a set of Leaf nodes and a set of candidate paths, and it may be provisioned on a controller, on the Root node, or on both.

Each candidate path is identified, in the context of the policy, by the tuple <Protocol-Origin, Originator, Discriminator> from RFC 9256, and the Root node selects the active candidate path using the tiebreaking rules of that document. A candidate path may carry topological or resource constraints and optimisation objectives that shape the tree instances computed from it.

A candidate path has zero or more tree instances. It has none when the controller cannot compute a tree that satisfies its constraints, and it can have more than one, for example during a Make-Before-Break change of the network state. One and only one instance MUST be the active instance of a candidate path, because two active instances would deliver duplicate traffic to the Leaf nodes. A tree instance is identified by an Instance-ID, an unsigned 16-bit number that is unique in the context of the policy.

The document updates the Replication-ID of the Replication segment control plane identifier defined in Section 2 of RFC 9524. It becomes the tuple <Root, Tree-ID, Instance-ID>, so that the Replication segments of an instance are identified in the control plane by <Root, Tree-ID, Instance-ID, Node-ID>. In the simple case where RFC 9524 uses a 32-bit number, the Root MUST be zero, the Instance-ID MUST be zero, and the 32-bit Tree-ID carries the value.
sections.plainLanguage: Each policy is named by the address of its entrance node and a 32-bit number. Each candidate path inside it is named by a three-part identifier, and the entrance node picks which one is active. Each tree instance has a 16-bit number, and only one instance of a candidate path may be active at a time, or the destination would receive the same traffic twice.

sections.title: Steering Traffic into a Policy
sections.content:
Traffic reaches the policy through a Binding SID (BSID), which is used when the Root node is not the ingress node of the SR domain where the traffic arrives. The packets are steered from the ingress node to the Root node with a segment list whose last segment is the BSID. The document recommends that the BSID stays constant for the lifetime of the policy, so that the steering of traffic to the Root node does not change, and it notes that the BSID may be the Tree-SID of the active instance of the active candidate path, in which case it changes whenever the active candidate path or the active instance changes. A BSID is not needed when the Root node of the policy is also the ingress node of the domain where the traffic arrives.

The Root node steers an incoming packet into a policy in one of two ways. With local-policy-based forwarding, the Root maps the packet to the active instance of the active candidate path using local forwarding policy, and replicates it with the encapsulated Replication-SIDs of the downstream nodes. The mapping itself is out of scope, but the document recommends that an implementation can show which traffic was mapped to which policy, candidate path and instance. With Tree-SID-based forwarding, the BSID in the incoming packet is used to find the active instance; the BSID is replaced with the Tree-SID of the active instance, and the packet is replicated with the Replication-SIDs of the downstream nodes.

For local-policy-based forwarding with SR-MPLS, the Root SHOULD set the TTL in the encapsulating MPLS header so that the replicated packet can reach the furthest Leaf node. It MAY instead take the TTL from the payload, in which case the copied packet may not survive the trip. For SRv6, the guidance for the IPv6 Hop Limit of the encapsulating IPv6 header is in Section 2.2 of RFC 9524.
sections.plainLanguage: When traffic does not arrive at the entrance node of the policy, the entrance sends it there using a Binding SID, a number in the packet that means go to this policy. The Root then decides which tree the packet belongs to, either by its own forwarding rules or by the Binding SID in the packet, and makes one copy for each branch of the tree.

sections.title: Inside a P2MP Tree Instance
sections.content:
A tree instance establishes a forwarding structure from the Root node to a set of Leaf nodes through a series of intermediate Replication nodes. It consists of a Replication segment at the Root node, zero or more Replication segments at intermediate Replication nodes, and Replication segments at the Leaf nodes.

Leaf nodes carry a complication. A service is identified by a service context in the packet, and a tree instance is usually associated with one multipoint service. On a Leaf node the transport identifier, the Tree-SID or Replication-SID of the Replication segment there, is also tied to the service context, because separating the transport and the service context is not always feasible with efficient replication in the core: multipoint services may have differing sets of endpoints, and a service context allocated downstream cannot be encoded in packets that were replicated in the core. In SR-MPLS deployments a controller MAY skip the Replication segments at the Leaf nodes when it is known that the services can be identified uniquely by their service label, and the Replication nodes upstream then remove the Tree-SID from the packet before forwarding it. In SRv6 deployments the Replication segments at the Leaf nodes MUST be instantiated, because the Tree-SID is carried in the IPv6 Destination Address field of the outer header and behaviour such as Penultimate Hop Popping is not feasible.

A Replication segment MAY be shared between different tree instances, for example to protect the adjacency or path between a Replication node and a common downstream node. A shared Replication segment is identified with a Root set to zero, an Instance-ID set to zero, and a Tree-ID that is unique within the context of the node where the segment is instantiated.

When a packet enters a tree instance, the Replication segment at the Root node replicates it and forwards copies downstream. Each copy carries the Replication-SID of the Replication segment at the downstream node. That node is either a Leaf, where the replication process terminates, or an intermediate Replication node, which replicates the packet again through its own segments until the packet reaches all the Leaf nodes. A Replication node and its downstream node do not have to be adjacent. For SR-MPLS, one or more SIDs are inserted before the downstream Replication-SID. For SRv6, the LOC part of the downstream Replication-SID can guide the packet to the downstream node, or a segment list can steer it along a chosen path.
sections.plainLanguage: The tree is made of one segment at the entrance, some in the middle, and one at each destination. A destination also has to know which service the packet belongs to, and because the two cannot always be separated, the number that steers the packet carries the service with it. In SRv6 that is unavoidable, because the number sits in the address field of the outer header. When the entry in the tree is not next door in the network, the packet is given extra directions to reach it.

sections.title: Using a Controller to Build the Tree
sections.content:
A controller is provisioned with the policy and its candidate paths, and it performs two functions: discovering the network topology across Interior Gateway Protocol areas, levels or Autonomous Systems, and discovering which nodes can take part in a policy and advertising that they can.

The controller then computes one or more tree instances for the candidate paths. It MUST compute a tree with no loops at steady state, as required by RFC 9524. It SHOULD modify an instance when it detects a change in the topology that affects the tree, or when a better path can be found from the new state. Alternatively it MAY use a Make-Before-Break approach to keep traffic loss small: create a new instance, activate it once it is in the network, and then remove the old one.

The controller assigns the Replication-SIDs, either dynamically or as they were set by whoever provisioned the policy. For SR-MPLS a Replication-SID may come from the SR Local Block or the SR Global Block, and the document recommends the local block, because Replication segments are local to each node of the tree while the global block is significant across the whole domain and could be depleted. It also recommends that the Tree-SID be used as the Replication-SID of all the Replication segments of an instance, which simplifies operations and troubleshooting, though the Replication-SIDs at the intermediate Replication nodes and the Leaf nodes MAY differ. The controller may reserve blocks for these assignments, or it may leave the Binding SID to the Root node.

To install the tree, the controller signals the Replication segments with a protocol such as PCEP or BGP, or with NETCONF/YANG or another mechanism; the exact procedures are out of scope. A node SHOULD report a successful installation, and SHOULD report a failure, preferably with a reason, for example when the Replication-SID conflicts with another SID on that node. If an installation fails the controller SHOULD try again, with an upper bound on the number of attempts, and if it still fails it SHOULD raise an alert, for example through syslog, and it SHOULD rate-limit those alerts. The controller SHOULD tear the instance down if the Replication segment at the Root node fails, and MAY do so when other segments fail. One way to bring an instance up quickly is to install the segments at the Leaf nodes and the intermediate Replication nodes first and the Root node's segment last, so the instance can be activated as soon as it is ready.

Protection comes in two forms. A link, node or replication branch can be protected locally with backup SR Policies, with a node-local Loop-Free Alternate or TI-LFA, or with a micro-loop prevention mechanism. For end-to-end protection the controller can build a disjoint backup tree instance, by computing a backup candidate path whose instances do not overlap those of the active one.
sections.plainLanguage: A controller learns the shape of the network, works out the tree, gives each node its part of it, and tells the nodes when the tree is ready to carry traffic. If a node refuses the tree, for example because the number it was given is already in use, the controller tries again a few times and then raises an alert. The tree can also be protected: one way is a second, separate tree that does not share any path with the first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document repeats the security considerations of RFC 9524 and adds its own. An SR domain needs protection from outside attackers, as described in RFC 8402, RFC 8754 and RFC 8986. Failing to protect an SR-MPLS domain by correctly provisioning MPLS support per interface lets attackers from outside the domain send packets to the receivers of the multipoint services that use the policies. Failing to protect an SRv6 domain with inbound Infrastructure Access Control Lists on external interfaces, or to implement the source address filtering of RFC 2827, has the same effect.

Incorrect provisioning of Replication segments by the controller can result in a chain of segments forming a loop, and the replicated packets then create a storm until the MPLS TTL or the IPv6 Hop Limit falls to zero. The control plane protocols used to install the segments, such as PCEP or BGP, can use their own security mechanisms such as encryption and authentication filtering. For SRv6, the document points out the exception in RFC 9524 for the ICMPv6 Parameter Problem message with Code 2: an attacker who injects a packet with the source address of a node and with an extension header using an unknown option type marked as mandatory can make that node send a large number of ICMPv6 Parameter Problem messages, which is a denial of service against the source node.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are the ones that already apply to a Segment Routing domain: filter traffic at the edge so that outsiders cannot pretend to be part of the tree. The document also warns that a badly installed tree can loop on itself, and that the protocols used to install it should be protected with their own authentication and encryption.
